title: Thoroughbred
wiki_lead:
The Thoroughbred is a horse breed developed for horse racing. Although the word thoroughbred is sometimes used to refer to any breed of purebred horse, it technically refers only to the Thoroughbred breed. Thoroughbreds are considered "hot-blooded" horses that are known for their agility, speed, and spirit.
The Thoroughbred was developed in 17th- and 18th-century England, when native mares were crossbred with imported stallions of Arabian, Barb, and Turkoman breeding. All modern Thoroughbreds can trace their pedigrees to three stallions originally imported into England in the 17th and 18th centuries, and to a larger number of foundation mares of mostly English breeding. During the 18th and 19th centuries, the Thoroughbred breed spread throughout the world; they were imported into North America starting in 1730 and into Australia, Europe, Japan and South America during the 19th century. Millions of Thoroughbreds exist today, and around 100,000 foals are registered each year worldwide.
Thoroughbreds are used mainly for racing, but are also bred for other riding disciplines such as show jumping, combined training, dressage, polo, and fox hunting. They are also commonly crossbred to create new breeds or to improve existing ones, and have been influential in the creation of the Quarter Horse, Standardbred, Anglo-Arabian, and various warmblood breeds.
Thoroughbred racehorses perform with maximum exertion, which has resulted in high accident rates and health problems such as bleeding from the lungs. Other health concerns include low fertility, abnormally small hearts, and a small hoof-to-body-mass ratio. There are several theories for the reasons behind the prevalence of accidents and health problems in the Thoroughbred breed, and research on the subject is ongoing.

Breed characteristics

The typical Thoroughbred ranges from 15.2 to 17.0 hands (62 to 68 inches, 157 to 173 cm) high, averaging 16 hands (64 inches, 163 cm). They are most often bay, dark bay or brown, chestnut, black, or gray. Less common colors recognized in the United States include roan and palomino. White is very rare, but is a recognized color separate from gray. The face and lower legs may be marked with white, but white will generally not appear on the body. Coat patterns that have more than one color on the body, such as Pinto or Appaloosa, are not recognized by mainstream breed registries. Good-quality Thoroughbreds have a well-chiseled head on a long neck, high withers, a deep chest, a short back, good depth of hindquarters, a lean body, and long legs. Thoroughbreds are classified among the "hot-blooded" breeds, which are animals bred for agility and speed and are generally considered spirited and bold.

Thoroughbreds born in the Northern Hemisphere are officially considered a year older on the first of January each year; those born in the Southern Hemisphere officially are one year older on the first of August. These artificial dates have been set to enable the standardization of races and other competitions for horses in certain age groups.


Terminology
The Thoroughbred is a distinct breed of horse, although people sometimes refer to a purebred horse of any breed as a thoroughbred. The term for any horse or other animal derived from a single breed line is purebred. While the term probably came into general use because the English Thoroughbred's General Stud Book was one of the first breed registries created, in modern usage horse breeders consider it incorrect to refer to any animal as a thoroughbred except for horses belonging to the Thoroughbred breed. Nonetheless, breeders of other species of purebred animals may use the two terms interchangeably, though thoroughbred is less often used for describing purebred animals of other species. The term is a proper noun referring to this specific breed, though often not capitalized, especially in non-specialist publications, and outside the US. grok_lead: The Thoroughbred is a breed of horse developed in England during the 17th and 18th centuries, renowned for its exceptional speed, agility, and stamina, primarily bred for horse racing. Its ancestry traces directly to three foundation stallions imported from the Middle Eastâthe Darley Arabian (imported around 1704), the Godolphin Arabian (arrived circa 1729), and the Byerley Turk (captured around 1688)âcrossed with native British mares to create a standardized racing stock. This selective breeding by English aristocracy resulted in a versatile athlete that forms the basis of the global Thoroughbred population, with all modern individuals descending from these sires. The breed's history is marked by the establishment of formal registries to preserve its pedigree and performance standards. The General Stud Book, first published in 1791 by James Weatherby in England, documented the lineage of racing horses and became the authoritative record for the breed. In North America, the American Stud Book was first published in 1873 by Col. Sanders D. Bruce and taken over by The Jockey Club in 1896, now maintaining a database of over 1.8 million Thoroughbred records, ensuring traceability and genetic purity through strict registration rules that require both parents to be registered Thoroughbreds. By the late 20th century, the annual North American foal crop peaked at 51,293 in 1986, reflecting the breed's widespread popularity, though numbers have since declined significantly, reaching around 18,000 as of 2023. Genetic studies confirm the Thoroughbred's maternal lineages derive from diverse Asian, Middle Eastern, and European horse populations, with mitochondrial DNA variability indicating a population expansion around 5,500â11,000 years ago, post-domestication. Physically, Thoroughbreds typically stand 15.2 to 17 hands high at the withers, with a lean, athletic build featuring a refined head, prominent high withers, deep chest, and powerful hindquarters that enable bursts of speed up to 35â40 miles per hour. They exhibit a spirited and intelligent temperament, making them suitable not only for flat racingâwhere horses begin competing at age two and peak around four or fiveâbut also for jump racing, steeplechasing, and even non-racing disciplines like eventing or show jumping after retirement. Common coat colors include bay, chestnut, black, and gray, though the breed's defining traits are its cardiovascular efficiency, with hearts weighing up to the equivalent of four bags of sugar, and daily water intake reaching 10 gallons during intense training. The global Thoroughbred racing industry, valued at over $115 billion as of 2008, underscores the breed's economic and cultural significance, generating substantial revenue through events like the Kentucky Derby and Royal Ascot.
